This study presents a novel time-series model called TD-PAR, a combination of the Poisson distribution and an autoregressive component with both immediate and lagging factors, to analyze and forecast count-based data over time. Theoretical advancements include deriving the conditional distribution of TD-PAR, enabling the estimation of parameters and forecasting the count-based data, and conducted a series of statistical analyses to evaluate the performance and reliability of TD-PAR-based forecasts.

While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions.

Numerous configurational molecular sampling methods such as Molecular Dynamics (MD) and Monte Carlo (MC) simulations rely on solving stochastic differential equations to update particle positions. Typically, these equations are solved using simple numerical methods like Euler's formula, which can introduce inaccuracies and bias the simulation outcomes. A more precise method, such as Kramers' equation solving scheme, might mitigate these issues but often does so at the expense of increased computational complexity. In contrast, our proposed approach utilizes the Langevin Dynamics to achieve precise simulation results with a minimum bias, by starting with high precision numerical methods like Malcuit-Scheiwe and then employing a novel configurational bias technique. As a result, we can achieve faster convergence and more accurate outcomes compared to existing methods, thereby enhancing the precision-effectiveness correlation for various systems, including Lennard-Jones and liquid nitrogen models, and demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach on complex biological systems like polyethylene and bovine insulin models.

We reevaluate the practice of using human-generated descriptions paired with images for training and evaluating automatic image description systems, highlighting concerns and alternatives. Our analysis shows that current evaluation methods may overestimate the performance of such systems and bias them towards producing safe but uninformative content. We propose using existing datasets in a way that prioritizes unique images and descriptions, and we suggest future research should focus on developing evaluation methods that account for both accuracy and diversity.

We use the concept of conformal field theory and its relationship with Euler-Arnold equations to explore new insights. A classification of conformal field theories based on the existence of a positive definite metric among vertex operators is presented, and we also examine the condition that allows for the computation of exact correlation functions.

Using the collective symmetry breaking approach, we forecast additional baryon and meson states that may appear as poles in the spectral function, thereby forming hadrons that decay quickly before decaying precipitously. We examine QCD's global symmetry group, specifically the transition from its asymptotic form to the nearly asymptotic form relevant for hadron physics, focusing on both light and heavy quark baryons and mesons. We utilize Bayes theorem to update our confidence in potential hadron states, considering both theoretical predictions and possible discoveries. Currently, we anticipate a wide range of additional heavy quark baryons and mesons, as well as certain light baryon and meson states, for which we predict mass ranges and possible quantum numbers.

This article presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IDED systems as alternatives to our previously proposed optimal wideband waveforming strategy in [1].
Fair-throughput and sum-throughput optimisation problems are defined and formulated.
By leveraging an algorithm that utilizes fixed points, we derive the optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput values for SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems.

Integrating vast amounts of data from experiments in particle collisions is the purpose of fitting programs for parton distribution functions, although this statement seems straightforward it hides the complexity of the process. As a wide variety of experiments contribute to this effort, drawing a unified picture of the way this data is analyzed is essential, which is the role of a theoretical framework for fitting parton distribution functions. This report serves several purposes: it reviews the underlying principles of fitting parton distribution functions, outlines the precise calculations required for different processes, discusses important issues arising from data integration, explains the implementation details of fitting programs, provides a summary of current parton distribution functions, and offers a perspective on future developments.

This study undertakes a linear analysis of a methane-air jet flame experiencing turbulence to determine its response to acoustic vibrations emitted from upstream, while factoring in temperature fluctuations that can cause instability in flames. To accurately predict flame behavior in a linearized model, it is crucial to account for heat released from the flame's fluctuations. Unlike previous studies, the current work utilizes an active flame approach that considers how heat released from the flame's fluctuations respond to acoustic vibrations. To apply this approach in a linear framework, combustion models must be linearized, which is shown to be challenging using existing models such as LES and DNS. Nevertheless, RANS models prove to be effective alternatives due to their ability to avoid closure issues. To apply these models, the researchers used LES to obtain the average flow conditions of the jet flame. An analysis of the results showed that a linearized RANS-Eddy Break-Up model yields the most accurate representation of reaction rates compared to other models, while an analysis of the model's equations revealed that reaction rate oscillations result from the disruption of Kelvin-Helmholtz vortex rings within the jet flame. Furthermore, the results from the model matched the outcomes from the LES simulations, confirming its effectiveness.

Nonlocal gravity theory is a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory. Based on an analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics, this new model involves a history-dependent relation that can be confirmed through data. The purpose of this paper is to provide a comprehensive overview of nonlocal gravity theory, including its fundamental frameworks and resulting constitutive relations. The underlying physical assumptions of this theory are also explained, along with necessary mathematical derivations and applications. The material presented here is unsuitable for a journal-focused on gravity research but may be suitable for a physics journal with a strong emphasis on fundamental theories.

This paper discusses the potential uses of minor systems in the LHC, which could serve as alternatives to the main detectors at the peta-scale upgrade. As ATLAS and CMS will be overwhelmed by data in the 2020s, these minor systems are proposed to exploit unused opportunities in the LHC physics program. They can operate in regions of the detector currently unused by the main detectors, such as the very forward direction, or employ novel detection techniques like photon-first or jet-first detection. These minor systems can target specific physics areas like low-pT electrons, low-kT jets, or central exclusive production, and can contribute to the discovery of new particles or verification of theoretical models. Furthermore, these systems may pave the way for future colliders like a 100 TeV machine and could serve purposes beyond high-energy particle physics, such as studying astrophysical phenomena or the properties of particles in extreme conditions.

Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit outbursts more frequently as they approach the point at which their radius matches their critical Roche radius. This idea is examined in this study by investigating the available data on the recurrence intervals of low mass neutron star binaries. A lack of short recurrence intervals was found, leading to an estimate that only a small fraction of neutron star binaries with low masses have outburst periods less than a decade. This information is crucial for defining a sample of neutron star binaries that is unbiased, which is necessary for accurately determining the black hole population within the Milky Way.

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number.

As technology continues to advance, reducing power consumption in computing systems has become an increasingly important goal. This research seeks to explore the possibility of decreasing CPU frequencies from gigahertz to megahertz ranges, a concept referred to as hyper-low power grades. To achieve this, several modifications are necessary, including changes to instruction set architectures, operating systems, and compilers. Furthermore, a new programming model is required to utilize the limited processing capacity of slow CPUs. This study presents an all-enabling framework called HyperDegrade, which incorporates multiple low-power grade CPU designs, each with unique characteristics, alongside a novel programming framework called HyperLock. By utilizing a linear programming approach, an optimal distribution of code can be determined to maximize overall system performance. Experimental results indicate that HyperDegrade outperforms existing low-power grade CPU designs by an average of 3.5 times in terms of overall performance, demonstrating the effectiveness of multiple low-power grade CPU designs in achieving hyper-low power grades.

We introduce a new algorithm called Delta-Split, which is a variation of the Split operation that can be applied to classical and welded links represented as planar diagrams. This new algorithm is more efficient than the existing Split algorithm, specifically in cases where multiple crossings require simultaneous resolution. In its most basic form, Delta-Split algorithm has a time complexity of O(n) in n crossings, which is an improvement over the conventional Split algorithm of the same name. Furthermore, we have implemented Delta-Split as part of a broader strategy called Delta-Theta, which incorporates both Delta-Split and Theta-Link algorithms to enhance the resolution of knotted links by resolving multiple crossings simultaneously.

In a system of multiple robots that perform tasks and share information with their neighbors, a strategy is proposed to accomplish a set of tasks that are not known in advance. The proposal assumes a network topology that is fixed and known, as well as information about neighboring robots that can be obtained quickly and cheaply. It is suggested that each robot can process limited information and communicate it to a neighbor at even greater cost. A simple algorithm is proposed that guides the robots in gathering and sharing information to accomplish tasks by optimizing their strategic decisions in a way that minimizes the cost of processing and communication. It is proven that this proposed strategy is the best possible outcome for these kinds of systems, as it eliminates the need for robots to spend time and effort exploring their environment in search of information.

In our study, we demonstrated how both a group that operates on a set in a recurring manner and a diagonal group are effectively incorporated into the wreath products under their combined, or product action, utilizing the Cartesian Breakdown approach.

The upgrade of advanced LIGO and Virgo interferometric gravitational-wave detectors involves replacing the current recycling mirrors with highly transmitting materials, which could potentially enhance sensitivity at high frequencies. However, doing so also introduces the possibility of unstable resonant oscillations, specifically the sloshing mode, which may compromise the stability and operation of the instrument. To address this challenge, a novel interferometer configuration known as the sloshing Sagnac topology is proposed, which utilizes multiple laser beams to stabilize the system and suppress the sloshing mode. Based on realistic parameters and simulations, this paper demonstrates that the sloshing Sagnac layout could provide improved high-frequency sensitivity compared to the conventional Michelson design, potentially allowing signal-to-noise ratio enhancements of over 50% for certain gravitational-wave events, without sacrificing low-frequency performance.

Recent large-scale MIMO systems are considered an exciting development, capable of providing rapid data transfer in crowded environments. As a result of their substantial size, MIMO arrays are subject to unique visibility constraints and areas that remain outside of their line of sight. With a high number of users often anticipated in applications of these systems, determining collision-free transmission times for users is a complex task. To address this challenge, a new protocol is proposed that takes advantage of fully and partially visible regions for simultaneous signal detection. At the beginning of the process, users with extensively visible positions are given priority in a slot-based schedule to ensure efficient waveform design. Furthermore, a simplified algorithm is introduced to determine the collision risk and optimize signal design within partially visible areas. By utilizing linear transformations and properties of subspaces, users with fully visible positions require no complex channel estimation, whereas users in partially visible positions only need estimation of specific channel components. As a result, the paper presents a unique visibility-based approach for signal design and detection, along with performance improvements in terms of access success rate, reduced collision occurrences, and optimized signal power.

Neural text generation models have excelled at predicting words based on context, but their performance can be hindered by their lack of understanding of grammar and n-gram language models' need for vast vocabularies. This research fills the gap between grammar and vocabulary size in n-gram language models, demonstrating that even smaller grammars such as unigram models can produce high-quality n-gram models with minimal vocabulary requirements. A novel approach called Residual Learning was developed to learn the parameters of n-gram language models using existing neural models, reducing vocabulary needs and enhancing grammar understanding. This research offers several contributions, including a sophisticated method for estimating n-gram language models, a new way of defining contextual word representations, and a framework for evaluating grammar knowledge in language models.

This investigation seeks to explore whether advanced techniques such as deep learning can effectively detect instances where optical scan technology is providing inaccurate vote tallies in an election, and if so, if these methods can be used to accurately re-count those tallies.  A novel approach called Informed OCR is proposed that utilizes information about the voting process to enhance the accuracy of tally corrections.  To evaluate the effectiveness of Informed OCR, the researchers conducted a small-scale experiment with a limited number of samples from a recent close election in a US county, and found that Informed OCR outperformed standard OCR techniques in identifying inaccurate tally instances.  However, due to the lack of publicly available data on election tally errors, the researchers were unable to engage in a larger-scale experiment to determine the method's practical utility for post-election tally reconciliations.  The Code for the paper is available at https://github.com/slsplash/iOCR.

A simplified computer model is used to investigate various global atmospheric circulation patterns in an Earth-like atmosphere by simulating and experimenting with different rotation rates and temperature differences between the equator and the poles. To better understand these experiments, various factors are re-cast in dimensionless forms to define a parameter space in which circulation patterns are mapped and classified. Notable patterns and trends emerge when varying rotation rate, as well as the rate at which heat and motion are transferred and released in the atmosphere. Similar patterns in circulation are found to occur under both laboratory and atmospheric conditions, when the curvature of the planet is considered. Baroclinic waves that behave similarly to those observed on Mars appear under specific conditions of temperature differences and atmospheric stability. Extremely fast planetary rotation leads to the formation of multiple jet streams on the poles, similar to the multiple jet patterns observed in gas giant atmospheres, and results in varying distributions of heat in the atmosphere with different rotation speeds.

This study formulates a range of integral representations for the reciprocal gamma function, stemming from its definition as a complex contour integral. We begin with the characteristic complex representation, followed by real representations involving single and multiple integrals, before concluding with an expression featuring a product of multiple integrals. Each of these formulations arises from the initial definition and involves dividing the contour integral into segments to address the poles of the function. As a result, we derive a series of real integral expressions for the reciprocal gamma function, meeting the research requirements following its initial publication with A. Erdely.

Researchers have developed a new theoretical framework, called phase-space RHD, to describe the dynamics of interacting Bose gases in a specific context. This method extends previous approaches, such as $1D$ hydrodynamics, by incorporating both $1D$ and $2D$ fluid dynamics and includes a comprehensive description of collective excitations and their coupling. The phase-space RHD framework resembles standard many-body theories, including Bogoliubovapproaches, yet offers a unique perspective by drawing comparisons with classical hydrodynamics. Theoretical studies have shown that the phase-space RHD method and the Bogoliubov theory share similarities in their outcomes, particularly in regards to the excitation spectra of interacting Bose gases, thus demonstrating its validity.

Deep Neural Networks have been highly effective in various tasks but their large size and complex computation processes make them difficult to implement in real-time on tiny devices. This problem has led to the concept of teacher-student learning, where a smaller student network learns from a larger instructor network. In this work, we review the teacher-student learning framework where the student network is initially unknown to the instructor, and through interaction with the student, the instructor guides its learning. We explore recent advances in tiny device implementations, examining aspects such as knowledge distillation, teacher design, and student optimization. Our survey discusses recent tiny device implementations of binary, sparse, and ultra-low bit-width neural networks, as well as recent research on tiny device-friendly architectures such as mobile phones and edge devices. We provide a comprehensive overview of teacher-student learning on tiny devices, analyzing trends, challenges, and possible solutions. We also outline promising directions for future research on this topic.

We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in graphical models, which serves as a foundation for a variety of computational tasks. Our new representation significantly reduces the complexity of specifying conditional distributions in these models, which often involves complex functions. particularly, we observe that tabular representations of functions are a key source of computational slowdown. To address this, we propose a novel brief tabular representation of functions, which we call a BFW. Our BFW framework markedly simplifies the computation of exact solutions for the most probable explanation (MPE) and constrained optimisation problems in graphical models. We demonstrate the practical utility of BFW by deriving a new algorithm for exact MPE computation, which we call the BFW-SG algorithm. This algorithm exploits the BFW representation to avoid the typical slowdown caused by conditional tables. As a result, we achieve significant improvements over existing methods, specifically the TRW-S algorithm, which requires excessive storage for complex functions. We further illustrate the exceptional scalability of the BFW-SG algorithm by applying it to a variety of benchmark datasets, which involve complex distributions and difficult inference tasks.

Recently introduced is a higher rank algebra known as the Racah algebra $R(n)$. A special variant, termed the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$, is then defined as a quotient of the Racah algebra by its central elements. It is then demonstrated that this $sR(n)$ algebra is equivalent to the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ through application of classical invariant theory, particularly with respect to a specific embedding of the Lie algebra $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ within a tensor product. As a result, the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ can be presented through generators and defining relations, offering an innovative perspective on its structure. Furthermore, a higher rank variant known as the special Askey-Wilson algebra $(sAW)_3$ is found to be isomorphic with the centralizer $Z_3(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ through the same principles of classical invariant theory, allowing an novel picture of its structure as well.

The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, paired-permutation testing is often criticized for its slow performance, which is attributed to the costly computation of scalar products. In response, we've developed a precise paired-permutation testing algorithm that exploits the structural properties of commonly used test statistics. By doing so, we've created an efficient framework that reduces the need for costly computations. In our experiments, we observed a significant improvement in processing time for paired-permutation testing, without compromising accuracy. As an additional contribution, we've released our code and a precomputed table of unique scalar product values to facilitate future applications.

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles.

This study develops a Poisson single-sensor Bayesian binary mixture (PMBM) filter for tracking objects, with a key innovation being the use of a partially grid-based origin model. The research introduces three possible scenarios for the initial distribution of the target, ranging from uniform to biased, and analyzes the optimal sensor activation strategy for each case. A Monte Carlo simulation is employed to compare the average estimation error of the filter across the three scenarios, with results showing that the partially grid-based origin model yields more accurate estimates. Furthermore, an analysis is conducted to assess the stability of the optimal sensor activation strategy in response to variations in measurement noise, with findings indicating that the strategy remains effective even in noisy conditions.

The dynamics of soccer games mean even small moments can greatly impact the outcome, making players, coaches, and scouts intensely curious about how to act effectively in pivotal situations. In such moments, players must decide between taking risks and attempting a shot or playing it safe and passing the ball to a teammate. To help guide these decisions, we propose a novel external assistant called "Strategic Kick" that can provide players with the best course of action in these critical moments. This assistant is based on a deep reinforcement learning algorithm that reviews numerous possible scenarios and outcomes, allowing it to make informed decisions about shooting or passing the ball. Our research finds that this algorithm outperforms common shooting locations on the pitch and even matches the shooting abilities of professional players in these situations. Therefore, we believe the Strategic Kick assistant has the potential to enhance player performance and contribute significantly to the growth of the soccer industry.

The development of sophisticated technologies has enabled the creation of large structures in laboratories for testing and evaluating complex phenomena. Unfortunately, even advanced facilities with numerous measurement points still struggle to accurately capture the intricate details of interesting phenomena due to limitations in probe placement and signal interference. This paper addresses this challenge by presenting a novel technique where a single-point Laser Doppler Velocimeter (LDV) system is used to obtain two-dimensional measurements of a mixing layer developing between two air jets with varying jet velocities. This approach leverages the inherent principles of laser interferometry and the concept of a mixing layer development to derive two-dimensional velocity distributions in the mixing layer, even when the probes cannot be placed within the area of interest. The proposed method is straightforward, requiring only minimal calculations and is thus suitable for immediate implementation in various applications.

We provide explicit definitions for the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves in a model that includes a Klein-Gordon equation and an anharmonic oscillator. We also conduct a comprehensive analysis of the linearized equation's spectrum at the solitary wave state.

Searching for lightweight bose-higgs bosons through missing energy signals in
  collison experiments at the belile II facility is complicated by background
  phenomena such as pair production of light feynman-x bosons and initial state
  radiation, as well as misidentified or missing detector signatures of final state
  particles like photons and neutrinos. To overcome these obstacles, a new search
  strategy is proposed that focuses on specific $B$ decay modes and utilizes the
  unique characteristics of the belile II experiment, such as the high energy of
  incoming electrons and the capability of the mdx pixel detector to identify
  neutral particles through their interaction with matter. By combining additional
  theoretical knowledge about the behavior of alps in electroweak splitting functions
  and the production processes of interest, further improvement is possible.
  Assuming a production cross-section of $10^{-6}$ pb and a decay constant of
  $10^{-3}$ ev, a statistics of $100$ ab$^{-1}$ is sufficient to detect alps
  with a mass of $10^{-1}$ meV and a production cross-section of $10^{-8}$ pb
  can be probed for a decay constant of $10^{-4}$ ev. A new approach to integrating
  ALP decay and production is also presented that avoids the use of weakly interacting
  long-lived particle theories.

This study conducts an in-depth examination of the effectiveness of several contextualized language models in detecting and identifying exact phrases that have been subtly modified in meaning. Our findings reveal that despite the promising performance of these models in various tasks, they exhibit a lack of ability to accurately detect semantically altered phrases when compared to tasks such as sentence classification. We attribute this shortfall to the nature of the tasks, which prioritize understanding in contexts where significant change has occurred, rather than pinpointing precise regions of the phrase that have changed. To address this, we propose a straightforward approach that utilizes these models to identify altered phrases, which involves determining if a generated sentence encoding the absence of a phrase slot is embedded in the vicinity of the phrase in the output of the model. This method proves superior to existing methods for identifying semantically altered phrases on a standard dataset, which we find to be ineffective. As an additional contribution, we release the dataset used in the study, which may benefit researchers in the field of natural language processing.

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), containing accreting black holes at their center, allow for the investigation of black hole mass and spin through the analysis of electromagnetic spectra. This research uses the Spin-Modified Fundamental Plane of black hole activity, a non-linear model that links radio luminosity, optical or X-ray luminosity, black hole mass, and spin. Accounting for uncertainties in luminosity measurements, the conversion of values, relativistic beaming effects, and the characteristics of the AGN system, we determine the minimum possible spins of heavy jetted AGNs. These results help explore the possibility of ultralight boson production through superradiance, based on the accumulation of empty mass gaps around black holes, as indicated by X-ray binary system Microlensing observations. We examine three heavy quasar black hole spin estimates: two main sources and one additional source, all leading to possible mass-to-spin ratios for ultralight bosons. Conforming to the standard model of particle physics, these ratios compare the fraction of hidden dark matter to hidden dark energy. We discuss several alternative theory predictions, including axion-like profiles, first-order phase transition scenarios, and certain composite particle models, based on the data obtained.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying in intensity or driving forces that changed over time. Calculations of position expectations were carried out for multiple scenarios of mass, angular frequency, and the lambda parameter in both cases. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions closely matched by both simulation methods. A discrete-time lattice Metropolis algorithm was used to evaluate the imaginary time path integral for these simulations.

We have developed a Hoare logic specifically for relational Hoare reasoning, suitable for both shared-state and distributed-state quantum programs. This new approach integrates relational Hoare reasoning with the methodology of expectations, enabling effective automation of quantitative evidence about program behavior. We have implemented our logic as a proof assistant module, using the Metitarski method to incorporate an unresolved solver for classical reachability properties. Additionally, we have applied our framework to several case studies, demonstrating its effectiveness by verifying complex quantum safety properties with minimal manual effort.

The paper addresses the problem of bias in vector magnetic field maps, particularly in estimating the component perpendicular to the line-of-sight, Bperp. This issue has been identified previously; however, the current study aims to provide a more in-depth analysis of its sources, quantification, and possible solutions. Initially, the authors establish precise metrics to assess Bperp bias, accounting for both local and native components. Secondly, various inversion techniques and data sources are tested and compared, incorporating a crucial factor called magnetic fill fraction (ff). A simple model is employed to evaluate the effects of noise and bias models. The results reveal that the bias primarily affects under-resolved structures but also manifests in areas with strong magnetic fields. Noise in magnetograms exacerbates the problem, but it's not the main contributor. The research indicates that fitting ff explicitly can significantly mitigate the issue; however, other factors like choosing appropriate chi^2 weights and optimization algorithms also play a crucial role. Finally, the authors propose a straightforward, post-processing correction that can be applied before resolving the 180deg ambiguity in Bperp. This approach is valuable for using global-scale structures as model boundary inputs. The study's findings advocate for employing inversion codes that fit ff directly or utilize data pre-processed in a similar manner, such as SyntHIA.

We establish that groups featuring involutions with a 2-closed Boolean centralizer system satisfy the conditions for a centralizer distribution to form a Boolean structure, as per the work of Tits and Tits-Chevalley. Moreover, we find that this Boolean structure takes the form of a tree once the conditions mentioned by Scott are met.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in a space with a time component, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in uniquely simple instances. A formula previously established for curves in a metric space is not applicable in scenarios involving a time component, thus a new formula has been derived to describe the second derivative of these curves.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant.

Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of interpersonal if-then relationships, comprising nearly a million statements from various perspectives, including causes, effects, positives, negatives, specifics, and generics. We have developed a range of AI techniques to process these statements, including models that predict relationship types, understand context, and perform inference. Our findings demonstrate the effectiveness of these models in multiple applications, such as conversational AI, sentiment analysis, and reasoning. We have also conducted a detailed examination of the statistics associated with slots, statements, and relationships. Our results indicate that both statement and relationship patterns follow power-law distributions. We have further developed an intuitive graph representation of the dataset, highlighting the hierarchical structure of relationships. Our technique for inferring relationship hierarchies yields a precision of 90% or higher for the majority of slots.

Our proposed approach tackles the challenge of new-view video prediction, taking input from a fixed vantage point. Unlike traditional methods that predict frames based on the current frame, our technique generates frames by estimating the view transformation first. This estimation leverages a dual representation, combining local and global information to produce a plausible perspective change. Our novel architecture consists of two separate networks, each processing different aspects of the representation. The local component uses a convolutional network to predict a deformed mesh, while the global component employs a 3D convolutional network to predict the depth map. After the perspective transformation, the predicted depth map is used to render the frame. Our model achieves remarkable results on real-world datasets, surpassing the state-of-the-art in terms of SSIM and PSNR scores.

A graph G is considered fully embedded in a metric space X if a distance in X can be uniquely defined for each pair of vertices based on their connectivity and distance in G. Previously it has been shown that a graph G is fully embedded in a metric space of dimension 2 if it's an infinite graph with a countable number of vertices or if it's a finite graph with more than one vertex at the same distance from any given pair of non-adjacent vertices. In this paper we introduce the concept of a trimmed metric dimension for graphs and demonstrate that a graph of a finite size is fully embedded in a metric space of the lowest dimension 2 if its subgraph containing an arbitrarily large number of vertices can be fully embedded in a space of dimension 1.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, this study proposes a new method called "DGN-Conv2d" that combines a deep generative model with a conventional 2D-CNN architecture to improve cardiac sound classification.  The proposed DGN-Conv2d framework is tested on noisy recordings with significantly improved accuracy compared to existing approaches.  The proposed framework also demonstrates real-world applicability by showing promising results on a large public dataset (PhysioNet/Computing in Cardiology (CinC) 2017 Challenge) and a self-collected dataset from a pediatric stethoscope.  The proposed DGN-Conv2d framework outperforms current state-of-the-art methods on both publicly available data and self-collected data, suggesting its potential for real-world cardiac sound analysis.

Observations of galaxies often rely on line ratios for gas conditions and chemical compositions, but this method's validity assumes emission is in equilibrium. For most cooling lines, this equilibrium holds, but may not be the case for $^{13}$CO and CI, which have low densities and temperatures. Using ALMA and HERA data, we found that CI $\lambda$8070 and CII $\lambda$1589 are not in equilibrium for most galaxies, as confirmed by theoretical models. This non-equilibrium is more pronounced in massive galaxies and those with higher star formation rates. Although this imbalance affects CII and CI observations, it does not impact their use for measuring gas temperatures and resolving the energy crisis for CII. However, this finding may aid in developing more sophisticated models that account for excitation conditions and underlying assumptions.

We establish a connection between the Asymmetric Simple Exclusion Process and a newly defined stochastic process where particles' velocities serve as the focus of interest. By mapping ASEP onto this velocity process, we derive a closed-form expression for the generating function of the velocity distribution, which in turn allows us to compute absolutely all moments of the velocities at stationarity.

This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods for model compartment analysis. A unified framework emerges, emphasizing the critical role that context, drawing from epidemiology, medicine, and biology, plays in informing both model development and analysis. By analyzing a specific example involving the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, we illustrate the importance of prioritizing biological reality, combined with statistical validation, when drawing conclusions from model data. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of our findings for future research priorities.

Determining whether the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the highest mass densities observed in galaxies is primarily due to feedback mechanisms or altered black hole activity has been a subject of debate. To explore the role of active galactic nuclei in forming the main sequence and the slope of the mass-star formation rate (M*-SFR) relation, an analysis of a local sample of galaxies was performed. The results showed that radio and optical nuclei have a significant impact on SFR measurements, particularly when using UV data, and can explain the observed flattening of the M*-SFR slope. Additionally, it was found that AGN activity is more prevalent in massive galaxies with low SFR-to-mass ratios and may contribute to the extinction of radiation from star-forming regions around black holes, reducing observed SFRs. However, since the sample examined local galaxies, further investigation is needed to determine if this effect is prominent at higher redshifts and among more distant galaxies.

This paper conducts a sentiment analysis across languages, examining the
emotional content of news articles using both few-shot and zero-shot learning
techniques. The primary objective is to categorize Croatian news articles as
expressing positive, negative, or neutral sentiment, employing a dataset from
Slovene. The underlying model is a multilingual BERT-based system, pre-trained
on three languages: English, Slovene, and Croatian. The paper investigates
various setups utilizing datasets from two languages and presents a straightforward
multi-task model to accomplish sentiment classification. The assessment involves
zero-shot and few-shot learning approaches within single-task and multi-task
experiments for both Slovene and Croatian.

We discovered evidence suggesting the planet's angular momentum is being transferred to the star through interaction with its atmosphere, potentially in the form of a planetary scale wind that wraps around the star's polar regions at high latitudes. This unusual jet stream pattern might be caused by an unseen massive planet within the star's outermost layer of gas or, alternatively, by the presence of a substantial planetary mass that has sunk deep inside the star following a past gas giant disappearance. To confirm our findings, observers are urged to search for signs of the hidden gas giant by looking for its gravitational influence on the planet's orbital pattern or through spectroscopic studies of the star's oscillation frequencies.

False news spreads rapidly on social media platforms, causing consequences for individuals and societies. The rapid spread of false information poses a significant challenge for verification processes, prompting the need for effective false news detection systems. This paper proposes a meta-learning based false news detection method that utilizes neural process networks and incorporates both text and image information from social media. A minimal amount of labeled data from a new event is all that is required to achieve high detection accuracy for false news, outperforming existing methods.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces by introducing a new concept called the "p-phase Golay complementary array" and derives explicit constructions for several previously unknown higher-dimensional Golay complementary arrays of order 12.

A system for generating synthetic brain injury data was developed using a progressive variational auto-encoded generative model, as per the NIST guidelines to ensure privacy is maintained.  The proposed method consists of multiple layers within the encoder, allowing the model to learn the underlying distribution of brain injury data quickly, drawing it from a variety of sources with diverse characteristics.  To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed method in creating high-quality synthetic data, various assessments were conducted, including but not limited to: confirming the statistical closeness between real and synthesized data, verifying the accuracy of machine learning models when using synthesized data, and ensuring there is no data leakage occurring during training.  The results showed the proposed method meets the requirements for generating high-quality synthetic data, as it enabled machine learning models to perform accurately when trained on synthesized data and demonstrated superior performance compared to existing variations of the AE model, including VAE, CVAE, and PGVAE, across all the conducted assessments.

Recent advances in feature extraction for neural networks have been highly effective, yet the existing frameworks that compare data points are complex and multifaceted, comprising multiple components such as data generators, neural networks, and optimizers, which are often highly customized and difficult to modify. In contrast, our proposed structure is remarkably simple, consisting of a neural network, an encoder, a encoder-neutral contrastive loss function, a optimizer, and pre-training and fine-tuning phases, which can be easily adjusted and refined to suit various scenarios and applications. The simplicity of our framework enables the development of novel contrastive learning techniques that utilize external knowledge such as taxonomy hierarchies, which can be employed to design features that reflect the perceived similarities and differences between data classes, resulting in enhanced performance by prioritizing features that distinguish between classes of interest.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, has yet to be examined. To bridge this gap, our approach develops a method to incorporate knowledge graph information into these models through training on a specific task. We demonstrate that LWMs can learn to retrieve information from knowledge graphs by drawing comparisons between existing approaches and our method. Our technique reveals notable improvements in retrieval performance on a standard knowledge graph dataset, outperforming existing methods. These results suggest that LWMs may utilize knowledge graphs to answer natural language queries, with our approach serving as a key precursor.

A thorough examination of a non-linear charged black hole, set within a non-linear electrodynamics framework and an anti-de Sitter (AdS) space, is conducted to determine its underlying physical mechanisms. We begin by exploring how this distinct structure responds to changing shade conditions, focusing on how energy transfer and redistribution occur among the black hole, surrounding fluid, and electromagnetic field. To achieve this, we introduce a new concept: the shade energy of the black hole. We then derive a precise equation that describes how the shade energy of this non-linear charged AdS black hole dynamically evolves over time in response to varying shade conditions. Furthermore, we analyze the role of non-linear electrodynamics in enhancing or diminishing the black hole's ability to accumulate and release energy under different shade scenarios. All calculations are supported by numerical simulations, ensuring the validity of our findings.

Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as entanglement and the onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances.

Researchers have examined the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ transition, as well as the evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay, by analyzing 1.7 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ of $pp$ collision data at 7 and 8 TeV. The decay chain $B^0_s\to D^0\bar{K}0_S$ is used to determine the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}0 K0_S$ branching fraction, which is found to be $(5.0\pm0.4\pm0.3)\times10^{-4}$. This measurement allows for the update of the CLEO branching fraction estimate for the $B^0_s\to D^0\bar{K}0_S$ transition.

Constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module is generally considered a challenging task. Despite the proposed method by Stanley to construct distributive lattices from their join irreducibles, determining all join irreducible submodules of a given module is not a straightforward task. However, for modules over lattices, a more efficient approach has been found by Bjorner and Stanley, utilizing the connection between submodule lattices and interval lattices of the underlying lattice lattice. When the module in question is simple, its lattice of submodules is isomorphic to its underlying lattice. Therefore, in this case, constructing its lattice of submodules boils down to computing interval lattices of the underlying lattice, a task that can be achieved using the underlying lattice's composition lattices. Given input submodules representing a subset of non-adjacent join irreducible submodules, we have developed an automated process to reconstruct the lattice of submodules of a module. This process begins with constructing the composition lattices of the underlying lattice, then mapping the input submodules to a portion of the submodule lattice, and finally deriving the lattice structure from this subset of submodules.

We explore how certain subsets of a higher-dimensional space are structured, specifically focusing on areas of lower dimension that minimize or maximize their volume within those subsets, under the assumption that their curvature is weakly positive.

A set is identifiable under the ratio $p/q$ if its identity can be confirmed by performing a subset of the given observations, modified by the same ratio $p/q$. We prove that non-degenerate sets are identifiable under the ratio $p/q$ if the denominator $q$ is larger than the number of distinct values a variable can take, and also establish a connection between identification efficiency for the ratio $p/q$ and binary identification for combined variables.

Using 13 TeV proton-proton collision data, specifically 1.7 inverse femtobarns of luminosity collected by the LHCb detector, the shape of the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^+\nu_{\mu}$ differential decay rate is determined as a function of hadron recoil. This rate is reconstructed via the $D_s^{-}$ decay sequence into $K^-K^+\pi^-$, following $D_s^{*-}$ decay into $D_s^{-}\gamma$. The resulting rate is fit with the underlying theoretical description, which includes contributions from weak interaction processes and relativistic corrections. The fit yields the $|V_{cb}|$ value: 42.24 x 10^-3, with a precision of 0.26%.

A persistent mystery in acoustic emission signals from cracking materials has been resolved by our research, who found a direct connection between these signals and the resulting fracture patterns. Through detailed analyses of both mechanical and optical data from peeling tests on a tape, we discovered that specific signal characteristics indicate the initiation of a new crack, allowing us to predict its outcome as either growth or closure. By mapping these patterns, we uncovered the underlying fracture network, demonstrating the potential of acoustic emission signals to serve as a real-time guide for controlling fracture evolution in materials.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems.

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformations that alter their input data. Our TPC framework comprises three distinct components: a dimension-reduced Gaussian smoothing strategy called TPC-G, an adaptive refinement mechanism called TPC-R, and an optimized search algorithm called TPC-S. By applying TPC-G initially to a substantial number of data points, we achieve significant time savings for the refinement process, which is then carried out on a smaller set of points using TPC-R. This refinement step serves as the base distribution for the search procedure, which we substitute with a simpler yet more efficient search strategy called TPC-S, which utilizes existing research called MAE. By incorporating kernel embeddings, we derive precise calculations for the trust boundary values without sacrificing accuracy. In our experiments on three distinct point cloud models, we observe notable improvements over existing methods in terms of the achieved reliability guarantees with no significant decline in model accuracy.

The process of testing programs has become increasingly complex, and the tools used to aid this process also grow more complicated. Despite the growing number of programs and their complexity, the amount of testing that takes place has not kept pace, and therefore, there is a pressing need to develop a testing method that is both efficient and effective. This paper introduces a new approach to program testing based on geometric concepts, specifically drawing on points and lines in a 2D plane. This methodology can be applied to both individual statements within programs and entire programs themselves, offering a framework for identifying both individual faults and more substantial issues. One of the key advantages of this method is that it can be automated using a computer, allowing developers to quickly and easily test their programs by utilizing a limited number of "test cases." In return, the authors were able to devise an algorithm that calculates the maximum number of test cases required for this method, which in many cases turns out to be very small. For example, according to the authors' calculations, testing a program consisting of 10 statements requires only 5 "test cases."

We provide a detailed explanation for a part of the Langlands program concerning the distribution of eigenvalues of automorphic L-functions, specifically for GL_2. This involves clearly defining the part of the weight distribution that we are addressing, in terms of the first Lyndon word appearing in the p-adic expansion of a CM field's discriminant.

Advanced composite materials with self-sensing capabilities are being explored for their potential use in critical structural applications. This study focuses on a phosphorus-nitrogen based polymer self-sensing composite material that changes electrical conductivity in response to damage. The goal of this research was to develop a method to accurately locate damage within these materials through exact shaping of electrical discharge energy. A genetic algorithm was combined with electrical impedance tomography to achieve this purpose. Initially, the technique was tested on a single-layer composite beam subject to a known point of impact. The results showed the presence of a point of impact could be effectively detected and its location pinpointed with high accuracy. Building on these positive outcomes, the researchers then applied the technique to a more complex multi-layer composite beam subjected to various impact locations. The results demonstrated the ability of the genetic algorithm to accurately locate points of impact even in complex structures. In one instance, the algorithm successfully pinpointed the exact location of a point of impact within a narrow area (2x10^-4 m^2) and its depth (within 10% accuracy). These findings suggest that genetic algorithms coupled with electrical impedance tomography have the potential to accurately locate points of impact in self-sensing composite materials.

This work proposes a tensor framework for Euclidean spaces based on geometric vector techniques and illustrates the method by transforming previous vector representations of the scalar product, the vector product, and the cross product into tensor forms.

A right-angled Artin group (RAAG) can be viewed as the fundamental group of a chamber system, consisting of at least 2 components that intersect trivially. We examine how this perspective relates to the structure of RAAGs, particularly in a component-based context, by analyzing how subgroups might split within this framework.

The development of high-performance algorithms for matrix inversion is particularly important for applications in signal processing, finance, and data analysis. Although faster than O(n^3) algorithms exist for lower order iterations, there is a lack of efficient higher order methods for matrix inversion that can utilize GPU acceleration. This research fills this gap by introducing novel algorithms based on higher order iterations that take advantage of sparse matrices and have improved memory coherence, making them exceptionally suited for GPU execution. The authors' most efficient algorithm, which utilizes 3rd-order iteration and -1.5 sparse matrices, demonstrates a significant performance boost over current gold standard algorithms by processing larger scale matrices and exceeding the performance limit of the current gold standard by an order of magnitude. As a result, the researchers are able to apply the higher order algorithm to a matrix of 20,000x20,000 size on a single GPU, setting a new benchmark in performance for matrix inversion algorithms.

Contextual linear bandits is an important model with various applications and has seen a significant surge in interest lately. This surge particularly occurred following the COVID-19 pandemic where learning in a distributed manner became highly coveted. Although numerous proactive studies have successfully utilized contextual linear bandits in various settings, most require the context to be shared publicly, posing a significant risk for sensitive information. In response, a new algorithm was recently introduced that enables learning without sharing the context but relies on an assumption that may not always hold true. On the other hand, contextual linear bandits with a fixed context set has numerous established learning methods that require minimal information about the context. These established methods could potentially fill the gap for context-based learning but require significant computational resources for large-scale contexts. In a significant breakthrough, a new approach was developed that combines these established methods with minimal information about the context to eliminate the need for sharing the context publicly on the server. Instead, context-based decisions can be made on an individual level without sharing the context publicly among agents. This new approach meets three criteria: it enables learning without sharing the context publicly, requires minimal information about the context, and allows context-based decisions to be made on an individual level without the need for communication among agents.

A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles develop and settle within these areas. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, impact the development and settling of particles, dust depletion might also suppress the VSI, as it limits gas cooling efficiency. In a research effort, we examine the potential stabilizing effects that particle growth has on VSI, focusing on a theoretical analysis and a created model that takes into account particle size development and settling behavior. Combining this model with stability calculations, we mapped areas in protoplanetary disks susceptible to VSI, analyzing its peak growth rates in various locations. As particles develop and settle around the midplane of these systems, VSI's reach diminishes due to decreased shear velocity. In a default model with a 0.01 solar mass disk, an enhancement from 10-micron to 1 millimeter particles reduces the VSI's growth rate by over ten times. As dust development restricts VSI-driven turbulence, it may encourage further dust growth, contributing to particle settlement seen in certain disks, including the HL Tau disk system.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional.

Recent advancements in computer vision have been slowed by the emergence of hidden functionalities inserted during training, which are triggered by specific input characteristics that aren't obvious to model outputs. These embedded features can lead to disappointing performance when models encounter new scenarios. A newly proposed architecture, global average pooling, has been found to be particularly vulnerable to incorporation of such hidden functions, which aren't accounted for in existing statistics. This discovery has forced the development of novel detection methods for these concealed features, although more research is needed to improve them.

In the context of a Parameter Server, learning from a distributed dataset on a graph G = (V, E) can be achieved through a random walk algorithm. Initially, a node s is selected to start the random walk, and a learning rate $\eta$ is chosen for updating the model. Each node v represents a local dataset dv, and an edge between nodes u and v indicates that their datasets are compatible for joint learning. The random walk algorithm from s visits each node v with a probability proportional to the size of the local dataset dv. The title "Stroll for Learning" refers to this random walk-based approach for learning from distributed data. A key aspect of this method is optimizing the starting node and the learning rate to maximize the accuracy of the learned model, which the paper achieves through an iterative process of bi-partite graph matching and learning rate adjustment. The authors introduce an efficient algorithm called "Stroll for Learning" that incorporates the random walk proximity measure into the optimization process, allowing the starting node to be an optimal node of the graph G that provides the fastest convergence of the learning process. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of the "Stroll for Learning" algorithm by conducting experiments on various real-world datasets and compares its performance to an existing optimization approach called "Learning from Local Repairs" (LLR). The results show that the "Stroll for Learning" algorithm outperforms LLR in terms of accuracy and has a significant advantage in reducing the starting node's degree in the graph

A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining interpolation methods to enhance semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed strategy uses consistency regularization to ensure the segmentation of mixed data matches the mixed segmentations. This approach belongs to the category of adaptive data regularization techniques that reduce overfitting when working with highly confident labelled data. The method has several advantages over alternative techniques such as adversarial and generative models, primarily due to its minimal computational requirements. Evaluations using publicly available MRI datasets - specifically ACDC and MMWHS - demonstrate that this simple proposed technique outperforms existing semi-supervised models, with source code available on GitHub.

In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns. We utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment to illustrate how the instantaneous non-locality of the wave function's collapse and single-particle entanglement can give rise to the phenomenon of steering, enabling a party to influence another's quantum state based on measurement decisions made by the first party. In this process, the spreading of the entangled wave function is exploited over vast distances, demonstrating how the non-locality of single-particle entanglement allows the particle to discern the detector used by the influencing party. Consequently, despite counterarguments, our proof confirms that single-particle entanglement results in genuine non-local effects between distant locations.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has yielded substantial benefits, albeit with heightened risks of security breaches and compromised privacy. As IoVs technology continues to evolve, there's growing interest in privacy preservation methodologies that adapt to these changes. Federated Learning has shown promise in safeguarding IoVs data and addressing concerns about security and privacy, whereas Blockchain technology presents possibilities for secure and verifiable data management. This paper conducts an in-depth review of Blockchain-based Federated Learning frameworks for IoVs, exploring potential problems, viable solutions, and future directions. This comprehensive survey can serve as a foundation for developing novel BC-FL approaches that address various IoVs data privacy challenges and scenarios.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in image/video recognition tasks, which involve high-dimensional data. In response, a new approach called Hierarchical Tucker Tensor Decomposition (HTTD) has been proposed that combines both hardware and algorithm levels to achieve high-performance and energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithm level, a compact LSTM framework is designed based on the HTTD structure, which reduces memory access delays and increases data compression. At the hardware level, a specialized HTTD-based LSTM accelerator is designed that includes multiple levels of memory hierarchies to match the HTTD structure, allowing for real-time frame recognition. Experiments have demonstrated the effectiveness of the HTTD approach in image/video recognition, with the compact LSTM framework exhibiting improved performance over existing compressed models and the HTTD-based LSTM accelerator showing significant gains in performance and energy efficiency over a widely used FPGA accelerator.

A polynomial function over a field of characteristic not 2 is called prime if its composite with itself cannot be expressed as a product of two other polynomial functions with finite image. We classify prime polynomial functions in a unknown constant field of characteristic not 2, based on their degree, and investigate the relationship between being prime and having a primitive root. Additionally, we examine the iterates of prime polynomial compositions and their application in prime factorization.

We investigate solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a non-linear interaction, within the scope of quantum mechanics, where a famous hypothesis proposes that solutions with negative energy will collide and combine. We examine this collision hypothesis by analyzing solutions that spread rapidly, forcing their disappearance from the functional space, within the area outside a complex shape that is smoothly curved. We achieve this by employing a recently developed technique that compares the shape of the solution to a known pattern, within a specific time frame, within a narrowly defined area around the shape's complex features. We then use this method to confirm the validity of the collision hypothesis within the proposed framework.

We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embeddings for a polynomial variety defined over a finitely generated $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra have an equivalent form to local positive-characteristic reductions of the variety.

Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the underlying statistical principles and the need for objective utility functions to make informed decisions. We explore various computational approaches and the resulting issues with Bayes factor estimates, including the reliability of bridge sampling and the limitations of numerical methods for evaluating marginal likelihoods. We also discuss the instability of Bayes factors in the face of model misspecification and the potential drawbacks of utilizing utility functions to resolve these problems. As a solution, we advocate for a thorough examination of model performance through diagnostic tools such as leave-one-out cross-validation, prior sensitivity analyses, and the assessment of model fit before evaluating hypotheses with Bayes factors. We illustrate the effectiveness of these strategies using a combination of synthetic data and real-world empirical research from the cognitive sciences.

Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate how discourse indicators convey meaning between sentences. Existing datasets used for classification tasks are insufficient for this purpose, so a new dataset, called DiscSense, has been created by drawing upon a widely used corpus. This dataset showcases instances of discourse indicators that demonstrate a proven pre-existing semantic connection between sentences. Furthermore, the paper contributes a straightforward method for analyzing the distribution of discourse indicators between sentences that has several benefits over current methods, including an automatically predicted classification system that can be used in classification tasks, a deeper understanding of how discourse indicators convey meaning, and a framework for mapping indicators to prepositions.

We develop a one-parameter extension of the Jordanian twistor space, incorporating the underlying Lie algebra of the BCK-algeids. This advancement enables us to derive a one-parameter deformed version of the Jordanian twistor equation, as well as its homogeneous counterpart. As a result, we can classify the underlying Lie algebra of the deformed Jordanian twistor space within the framework of infinite-dimensional Lie algebras, specifically within the class of associative Lie algebras.

We extended regular expressions with the alternation operator to address a security vulnerability affecting systems that utilize regular expression-based constraint solving. Our enhanced framework, extending regular expressions with the alternation operator, meets the requirements of (1) a theoretical foundation for the solvers and (2) practical utility for the solvers. We developed a new algebraic treatment for the extended regular expressions to underpin an automated proof procedure for their equivalence. Building upon this new treatment, we derived a first-order logic translation for the extended regular expressions. Furthermore, we enhanced the existing model-reduction technique to handle the alternation operator. Our comprehensive automated testing demonstrated the efficacy of our approaches by using them to solve complex constraints and determining the soundness of the approaches.

Building upon previous work by \cite{Ferrara:1971vh}, \cite{Ferrara:1973vz}, we develop a comprehensive integral representation of conformal block operators in CFT$_2$, specifically tailored for spinning primary fields. Notably, this integral expression can be re-expressed as a product of two weighted AdS$_2$ field combinations when the primary fields in question are conserved, which results in the representation of conserved current conformal block operators in CFT$_2$ in terms of geodesic operators defined within the AdS$_2$ framework rather than the AdS$_3$ framework. Moreover, this new perspective enables a direct link between the AdS$_2$ geodesic operator representation and massless higher-spin fields in the AdS$_3$ framework, facilitated by the HKLL bulk field reconstruction method. By harnessing this new picture, we are able to derive a closed-form expression for the four-point conformal block involving spinning primary fields as a product of two AdS$_2$ geodesic Witten diagrams.

To achieve high-resolution imaging with wide-field X-ray telescopes, a common issue arises when multiple mirror segments, each sensing a different area of the sky, overlap in the detector. This problem is particularly pronounced in missions featuring many large, curved mirrors, such as the future Large Wide Field Infrared Oven Digitizers (LWFM) telescope. Resolving this sensing conflict is crucial for determining the exact portion of the sky that has produced X-rays detected by the detector. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach based on the use of lobster-eye (or tank) optics, which can redirect X-rays onto different segments of the detector to pinpoint the source of the signal. We outline a possible design for this optics system, which we calculate will effectively increase the surface area of the detector by a factor of 20. Additionally, we conduct a simulation to demonstrate that this system can efficiently pinpoint the source of the signal, allowing the most sensitive detector segment to be used for the highest resolution imaging.

To investigate the relationship between the cosmic velocity field and the dark matter halo mass function, a comprehensive analysis was conducted. Using a variety of N-body simulations, a convolutional neural network was trained to predict the halo mass function based solely on the velocity field, drawing on 20 distinct simulation models spanning a wide range of parameters. The results showed that the halo mass function is influenced by the velocity field, with a significant impact observed on the low-mass halo end. Additionally, the analysis revealed that the velocity field's effect on the halo mass function is closely tied to its interaction with the dark matter density field, with the most substantial impacts occurring in regions of high velocity dispersion. An attempted fit to the predicted halo mass functions using a commonly employed model proved inadequate, highlighting the importance of the velocity field's role. An enhanced model was proposed, incorporating the linear combination of the density and velocity field fluctuations, which successfully described the halo mass function across all simulated scenarios, demonstrating its universality.

One of the key challenges in using atomic interferometry for measuring local magnetic fields is overcoming the minimal measurable value of the technique, especially when dealing with very weak fields. A novel approach has been proposed to address this issue by combining atomic interferometry with the Meissner effect of superconducting materials.
