The method takes advantage of the repulsive force between a superconducting material in its Meissner state and atomic coils, which enhances the sensitivity of the atomic interferometry by exerting a force proportional to the distance between the coils and the superconducting material. Theoretical models have been developed to understand the dynamics of atomic interferometry when it overlaps with a superconducting material, which has a critical temperature of 90 millidegrees Kelvin. Based on these models, a sensitivity analysis was conducted to optimize the parameters of the atomic interferometry system. The results showed that the combination of atomic interferometry and the Meissner effect can significantly improve the sensitivity of the technique, enabling the measurement of local magnetic fields as weak as 20 nanoteslas at the wavelength scale of the atomic interferometry. The proposed method has the potential to contribute to precision measurements of local magnetic fields and could also be applied to the study of gravitational waves in the millihertz frequency range.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn clusters on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of a single Mn adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while larger clusters exhibited localized YSR state splitting. Additionally, by scaling the exchange field, the absence of a gap in the YSR state spectrum at the edge of the superconducting gap was explained. Realistic and realistic-plus U interactions were compared, demonstrating the significance of localizing the correlated d-states of the impurity atom.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images to diagnose skin cancer. Our approach combines a convolutional neural network with an outlier detection method using entropy, thereby allowing for the identification of unusual data points that may be mislabeled. Although we were not ranked first, our techniques demonstrated exceptional accuracy and have practical applications in medical diagnostics, particularly in situations where large amounts of labeled data are not available or of high quality.

Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and resemble weak boson colliders beyond a few TeV, a new perspective is taken that treats weak bosons as fundamental components of these leptons. Within this context of a muon collider, we evaluate the relevance of W and Z particle distribution functions, particularly at their leading order in 2-to-n particle interactions. A thorough examination of both universal and near-universal adjustments, specifically power-law and logarithmic corrections, is carried out to determine the derivation of (polarized) weak boson distribution functions when approaching a limit of collinearity. A survey is also conducted to analyze multiple 2-to-n particle interactions at 2-to-30 TeV energy levels through weak boson fusion/scattering in both polarized and unpolarized conditions. A key contribution of this study involves the public integration of Effective W/Z and Weizs\"acker-Williams Approximations, collectively referred to as the Efficient Vector Boson Approximation, into the existing event generator software MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO, setting the groundwork for developing matching prescriptions between EW parton showers and EW distribution functions, and providing actionable advice on the use of W/Z PDFs to facilitate this development.

We bring together four landmark results by Godel, Tarski, Carnap, and Rosser, and present their proofs in a unified format. Tarski's Undefinability Theorem for arithmetic is proved using a first-order axiomatization, and we also provide a straightforward proof that the theorem holds for any recursively enumerable theory. Additionally, we establish the diagonalization lemma, which lies at the heart of these four results, in several different frameworks: first-order logic, second-order logic, and a logic of names.

This paper investigates the concept of invariant sets in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. A key theorem in the field relates the invariance of a set to the behavior of solutions when considering a line segment in phase space. We modify the theorem to suit fractional order dynamical systems by replacing the line segment with an invariant curve. A special case involves a circle, which we use to extend the theorem to include circular invariant sets.

Reconstructing the source signal inside a cavity when hearing its output through a nearby structure has applications in noise source identification and sound quality enhancement. Despite the growing interest in structural acoustic interaction problems, there's a lack of effective methods for reconstructing the source signal within a cavity by observing the vibrations of an adjacent structure. This study addresses this shortfall by introducing a novel approach that uses the observed structure vibrations and the theoretical model of a structural acoustic interaction to reconstruct the source signal inside the cavity. A key component of this method is the derivation of an analytical formula for the source signal reconstruction, which can be implemented using the available commercial numerical solvers. Furthermore, this paper has a companion website that provides a numerical solver as well as a MATLAB code for the source signal reconstruction, along with several example data sets.

Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we examine the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino characteristics, and dark matter behavior. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest scoto-seesaw framework, we establish a comprehensive understanding of particle spectra, mixing angles, and dark sector parameters. Notably, we determine the parameter ranges that meet theoretical requirements, satisfy dark matter relic formation, and comply with experimental limitations. Furthermore, we explore the connections between neutrino mass hierarchy, dark matter properties, and the weak scale stability. By incorporating the simplest scoto-seesaw model into the effective potential, we analyze the minimum temperature at which the electroweak vacuum state becomes stable during the early universe. Our findings reveal that the dark sector's impact on the weak scale stability is negligible; however, we observe a notable influence on the low-energy neutrino properties. Consequently, we identify a distinct region of parameter space that allows for a dark matter relic density consistent with observational data, while also meeting requirements for the neutrino mass hierarchy and the weak scale stability.
